assessment.summary: A present, quantified concentration risk — a single country supplies the U.S. with a major share of over a third of the minerals it most depends on importing, and the value of U.S. net imports of processed metals and materials more than doubled in a single year — that has already produced real supply shocks and price spikes, with escalation to a broader multi-country industrial disruption a live risk.
assessment.timeframe: Ongoing and worsening; the U.S. critical minerals list and import-reliance figures are reassessed annually, and 2025 saw China's export controls disrupt automaker production, cut indium export volumes sharply, and double the value of U.S. processed-mineral imports.

claims.text: The U.S. remained reliant on imports from China as a major source for 14 of the 33 critical minerals for which the United States most depends on imports (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026).

Net imports of processed metals and materials more than doubled by value, from $77 billion in 2024 to $185 billion in 2025, and the Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 covers 14 minerals, from antimony to tungsten, that China restricts exporting to the United States (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026).

The Department of the Interior's final 2025 List of Critical Minerals, published November 6, 2025 by USGS, identifies 60 minerals vital to the U.S. economy and national security whose supply chains face potential disruption risk, adding 10 new minerals — including copper, silver, and uranium — to the list.

China is the leading global producer of indium, accounting for 70% of the world total; the United States recovered no indium from ores in 2025 and its net import reliance was 100% of estimated consumption (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, February 2026).

In February 2025, China's Ministry of Commerce subjected several critical minerals, including indium, to new export restrictions; USGS reports Asian Metal data showing that exports of unwrought indium declined by 72%, year over year, from September 2024 to September 2025 (USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026, February 2026).

description: The energy, defense, and technology sectors depend on a small set of minerals whose mining and, especially, refining are concentrated in a handful of countries. Export restrictions, geopolitical tension, or a shock to a single dominant supplier can disrupt processed-material flows worldwide with little substitution available in the short term, as China's 2025 export controls on rare earths and antimony already demonstrated by forcing automakers to cut production and sending prices sharply higher. Indium shows the pattern in miniature: China produces 70% of world supply, the United States recovered none from its own ores in 2025, and unwrought indium exports fell 72% year over year after Beijing added the metal to its February 2025 restrictions.
name: Critical Mineral Supply Chain Disruption
